subject: astronomy
title: Spectra Calculations
welcome_lead: Use Wien's law and spectral patterns to extract temperatures.
meta_desc: GCSE Astronomy: Wien's law, peak wavelength and spectral line analysis.
final_note: A star's spectrum tells you its temperature, composition and motion.

concepts.def: Hotter blackbodies peak at shorter wavelengths.
Idealised object emitting based only on temperature.
Wavelength at which star emits most light.
Wavelength change due to motion towards or away.
Spectral lines shifted to longer wavelengths.
Spectral lines shifted to shorter wavelengths.

walkthroughs.body_html: Peak wavelength multiplied by temperature is constant: lambda_max * T = 2.9 x 10^-3 m K. So a hotter star peaks at shorter (bluer) wavelengths.
If a star peaks at 500 nm = 5 x 10^-7 m: T = 2.9 x 10^-3 / 5 x 10^-7 ~ 5800 K — a G star like the Sun.
Compare star's absorption lines to lab values. If shifted to red, star moves away. If shifted to blue, star moves towards us. Andromeda's spectrum is blueshifted because it is approaching us.

Lunar eclipses are more dangerous.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between a solar eclipse and a lunar eclipse?
options: In a solar eclipse the Moon blocks the Sun; in a lunar eclipse Earth's shadow covers the Moon.
Whether it has planets.
Solar eclipses happen by day, lunar at night - that is the only difference.
Lunar eclipses are more dangerous.

mcqs.q: What determines whether a star becomes a white dwarf or a neutron star?
options: Its colour during its main sequence phase.
Lunar eclipses are more dangerous.
Whether it has planets.
Its mass - low/medium mass becomes a white dwarf; massive stars produce neutron stars or black holes.
